Her heart-check (8 vs 13) faltered: at about the fortieth name her voice caught and the rite stalled mid-litany. The door shudders, the heartstone is hot, the sleeper stirs grieving, not yet angry. entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

The warding settles over Corm like a pale light, and he draws one long breath. Your voice carries the Morninglord's invocation out along the cold gallery, and then the names begin, slow and even, one by one into the iron.

For thirty-nine names it goes well. The stone under Corm's palm warms, and a deep note answers each name like a heartbeat. Then you reach the fortieth, a woman's name your own father-in-faith used to hum over bread, and something in the cadence slips. Your voice catches. The rhythm breaks, and the note under the iron rises sharp and uneven.

The door shudders in its frame. Dust sifts from the lintel, and the heartstone flares hot enough that Corm hisses through his teeth, but he does not take his hand away. The seal gives a long, low groan, not of rage but of something very old being woken in the middle of a dream. Cold, sweet air breathes out of the seams, and with it, faint and awful, a sound like many people sighing.

Hild has gone white. Garrick has an arrow nocked at the bend without having drawn it unstrung. Your Protection from Evil and Good still holds Corm, with about eight minutes left, and the rite is stalled at name forty of sixty, with twenty names left and Brenn's the last.

You have two spell slots, Channel Divinity, and the ledger open in your hands. What does Brun do?

She is optimistic, tries to find common ground even between fierce enemies, is suspicious of strangers, and wants to repay the mercy she was shown by walking into danger to keep others alive (ideal: Charity). Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

The warding settles over Corm like a warm hand, and he draws a long breath. You open the book, set your holy symbol to the iron, and begin.

The Morninglord's invocation comes easily. The names follow, one after another, each falling into the cold gallery like a stone into still water: the sixty, in the captain's order, and a slow, answering warmth gathers in the iron with every one. Hild's lips move with them. Garrick has taken off his hood.

Then you reach the fortieth, and the captain's ink is smeared by damp. You read what you think you see, and it is wrong. You feel it go wrong, like a foot placed on a missing stair.

The door shudders. The heartstone flares white and then dims to an uneasy ember. A deep sound rolls up from below, not a roar, but a long, frightened moan, the sound of something old being woken in the dark and not knowing where it is. Frost races across the iron bands. Corm's arm shakes to the shoulder, but the ward holds him, and he does not take his hand away.

"That's not the name," he says through his teeth. "Ansgrim's son. It was Ansgrim's son, Dorek, not Dorn. Say it right, Stonehearth. Say it gently. It's afraid."

Beneath the door the moan comes again, closer to the iron. The dread in it is plain, and you know exactly what it is to wake under stone and not know who is coming. Your protection holds for about nine more minutes. You have two slots left, and Channel Divinity, and the rite half-spoken.

input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4: The Naming spoken true (Religion 17). Brun cast Protection from Evil and Good on Corm. The sleeper (stone-spirit) answered, was named and released with mercy; the door opened of itself. The sixty's remains lie in the lower galleries to be carried up and buried. Brun awarded 200 XP. entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

The ward settles over Corm like a thin pane of light, and his shoulders ease a hair's breadth. Then you begin.

The Morninglord's invocation comes first, and the iron under your holy symbol warms. You speak the names slowly, one at a time, the captain's order, each set down like a stone on a cairn. At the tenth, the heartstone's low hum answers in a softer key. At the thirtieth, a faint warmth runs out of the door and along the gallery walls. By the fiftieth Hild is weeping without a sound, and Garrick has taken off his hood at the bend.

You reach the last name. "Brenn Ironvein," you say, "who walked in of his own will, and held its hand."

For a breath nothing moves. Then the stone's slow breath catches, lets go, and rolls out of the door as a long sigh. It is not sweet and it is not foul. It is only the sound of something very old being, at last, allowed to put down a weight. Corm cries out once, softly, and does not take his hand away. The iron bands go warm and then still, and the great door swings inward of its own accord, silent on forty winters of rust.

Beyond it is a stair, dry and clean, running down into a deep amber glow, like a banked fire seen through a window. Faintly, as if from a long way below, you hear what might be sixty voices letting out one breath together.

Your Protection from Evil and Good has run its ten minutes and you let it lapse, and no harm came. Hild takes a step toward the stair, and Corm, his face wet, catches her sleeve and then lets it go. "Go," he says. "Bring him up."

You earned 200 XP for the rite, which brings you to 900: you can take level 3. The sheet also shows a few items I did not narrate, an iron ring braided with auburn hair and two sealed letters to the Deepwatch, and I will leave them to you to tell me about.

Would you like to level up now, or first go down the stair with Hild?

Your hand settles on Corm's shoulder, the warding light of the spell lies pale gold across his scarred arm, and you begin. The Morninglord's invocation comes first, steady in the cold air. Then the names, one at a time, as if each were a stone set gently in a wall.

At the twentieth name, the iron door sighs. At the fortieth, the hum rises in your breastbone and something vast and slow turns over in the dark, a grief as old as the seam it was cut from, and you feel it lean toward you like a tide. You hold. You say the names plainly, and you do not look away. Corm's knuckles whiten on the stone, but the light on his arm does not flicker, and nothing touches him.

At the sixtieth name you say, "Brenn Ironvein," and Hild makes a small broken sound behind you.

The hum falls away. The iron bands warm, then loosen, and the door swings inward on a breath of cool, clean air that smells of wet stone and rain. Nothing rushes out. Only a long, quiet sigh passes over you, like a hand lifted from a shoulder, and the lamp flames lean toward the open dark and stand straight again.

Corm weeps without sound. Hild takes her crossbow from her back, looks at it, and sets it carefully on the floor.

You have earned the rite's 200 XP, which brings you to 900, enough for level 3.

entries.text:
Maren is quiet for a few paces, and then she talks, a little at a time, the way one lets out a rope.

The Deepwatch, she says, is cut into the face of a high crag, with one stair of three hundred steps and no gate at the top, only a bell that is rung once for every warden who dies. Inside is the Hall of Names, where the ledger-copies of every hold and the names of the lost are kept, and a council of old wardens, of whom she is one of the oldest and sourest.

About your mother, she gives you small things, and you take each like a coin. Sigrun climbed that stair on her hands for a wager when she was nine. She loved honey-barley cakes and sour apples. She hummed a miners' counting song while she drew her maps, and could not carry a tune to save her life. Once, to win an argument, she mapped an entire gallery by touch in the dark, and was right to the pace. "Stubborn," Maren says again, and this time it sounds like a blessing.

You find you are laughing, and wiping your eyes, and walking easier than you have in years.

The waymark-hut sits in the saddle as Garrick promised, low and squat, roofed in turf, with a stone hearth and a dry woodstack someone has kept filled. You cook, as you said you would: oatcakes crisped on the hearthstone, dried apple stewed with a little honey from Maren's pack, and broth from the innkeeper's flask. Garrick eats three helpings without a word and then, gruffly, says it is the best meal he has had since his mother's. It is a little before six, the light long and gold across the saddle.

In your pack, as you lay out the blankets, your hand finds the two sealed letters the sheet says you carry, Father Dorrin's, addressed to the Deepwatch in his cramped hand and never sent. Maren sees the seal across the fire and goes very still, but does not ask.

You have a full night ahead and no trouble in sight. What does Brun do?

entries.text:
Maren talks slowly at first, as if each memory has to be lifted out carefully, and then it comes easier.

The Deepwatch, she says, is a hall cut into the face of a granite cliff above a cold tarn, with a bell-tower, a record-vault the wardens call the Long Shelf, and a gate that opens only to a spoken kin-name. About forty wardens remain, most of them as old as she is. "You'll be the youngest face there in thirty years," she says dryly.

Of Sigrun she gives you small things, and you take each one like a coin. She loved honeyed barley cakes and sour plum preserve. She hummed a work-song called "Lamp and Line" while she measured, always slightly off the tune. She could not abide being indoors past noon, and she chalked a tiny sun on every survey stone she set. As a girl she climbed the bell-tower in the dead of night to see whether the stars were closer from up there. "They were not," Maren says. "She was furious. She went again the next night to be sure."

You laugh, and your laugh catches, and Maren does not look at you, which is a kindness.

By half past six you reach the waymark-hut, a low turf-roofed shelter of fitted stone in the lee of the saddle, with a hearth, a woodpile left by some earlier traveler, and a hammer-and-three-lines carved over the lintel. You cook as promised: oats, dried apple, a little salt pork from Garrick's pack, and the last of the innkeeper's wife's cheese melted over the top. Garrick eats two helpings without comment, which you take as the highest praise.

While you are unpacking your bedroll your fingers find something you do not remember, two folded letters sealed with plain grey wax and tucked into the back cover of Father Dorrin's prayer book. They are addressed in his cramped hand to the Deepwatch. The seals are unbroken.

The fire crackles, the wind moves over the turf roof, and Maren watches you across the flames without asking.

entries.text:
Maren is quiet for a few strides, as if she must go a long way back for it. Then she talks, and the road goes by without your noticing.

The Deepwatch, she says, is cut into the face of a high crag, entered by a long stair under a lintel carved with the three-stroke sign. Inside there is a great hall of ledgers, a hearth that has not been let go out in four hundred winters, and a wall where the names of the lost are cut, row on row. Only a few dozen wardens keep it now. "The Reckoner keeps the records," she says. "A sour old stick. You will like her."

Of your mother she says more. Sigrun hoarded honey-oatcakes as a girl and hid them in survey-tubes, so that more than one apprentice opened a tube expecting a map and found crumbs. She could not carry a tune to save her life, except one: a three-note thing she hummed under her breath while she worked, which the wardens called the plumb-line song. She left the Deepwatch young to survey the hill-holds because, Maren says, she could not abide a roof for long. "You don't like a roof much either, I'd wager."

You laugh, and it surprises you. Garrick, a few paces ahead, does not turn, but his shoulders move.

You reach the waymark-hut at the saddle a little after six: a squat dry-stone shelter with a turf roof, a hearth-stone, and a stack of dry peat someone has left for travelers, as wardens always did. The wind has dropped. You cook as promised, oatcakes crumbled into a pot with the last of the innkeeper's wife's dried apple and a shaving of hard cheese, and it is better than it has any right to be. Garrick eats two helpings and says "Good" in the tone of a man giving a medal.

Outside, the first stars are out over the hills. It is a little past six, you are at full strength with three spell slots and Channel Divinity ready, and the hut is warm. Tomorrow and half the day after lie between you and the Deepwatch.

The sentry says nothing for a long breath, and the wind fills the silence. Then the lantern swings away and you hear her shouting down the wall in Dwarvish, thin and fast. He looks at Maren first, then at the ring on your finger, then at your chin.

"Show me," he says gruffly.

You hold out the captain's ledger in its dry cloth, and with it, from the prayer book's back board, the two sealed letters in Father Dorrin's cramped hand that you found tucked behind the cover, addressed in plain Dwarvish to the captain of the Deepwatch. "Come in out of the rain, Stonehearth. Your mother's lamp is still lit on the seventh gallery."

Behind him, up the long stair, you can see a single steady light burning above all the rest.

For a long breath there is only the wind and the rain drumming on the bronze. Then the sentry's lantern swings away from your face, and you hear her shout down into the mountain, one word, over and over: "Sigrun's! Sigrun's! Sigrun's!"

Gods help us all, that is her jaw."

Maren sags against you, laughing and weeping at once. "Torvald," she says, "you old goat, I brought her."

Captain Torvald Greycairn looks at you for a long time, and then at Garrick, who has stopped dead in the doorway with his bow lowered and his hood back. "Your friend," Torvald says. "He is welcome too. Bring the ledger in out of the weather, girl, and bring that book. Whatever Dorrin put in the binding of it, I will read it by my own fire."

You startle, because you had never opened the binding. But when you take the book from your pack, the spine gives under your thumb, and between the leather and the boards two small, flat, sealed letters slide into your palm, both addressed in the old priest's cramped hand to *the captain of the Deepwatch*. He must have sewn them in a long time ago, against the day you finally came.

Behind you the storm breaks in earnest. Ahead is the warm gold hall, with its seven galleries and its Hall of Names, and a captain waiting at the fire. You are at 21 of 21, with three slots and Channel Divinity ready.

line:
Brun squares her shoulders, wipes the rain from her face, and calls up to the sentry in clear Dwarvish, "I'm Brunhilde Stonehearth, Sigrun's daughter, raised by Father Dorrin Ashbeard. I carry a copy of the Hearthdeep warden-captain's ledger, and I've come home."

She keeps one hand on Maren's arm and glances at Garrick. "Stay close, friend. You're with me, and you're welcome here."

input.description: Captain of the Deepwatch. Stern, broad, iron-grey dwarf with a cairn-stone pendant, Maren's old rival and only friend. Objected to Sigrun's marriage to a lamp-maker who would not swear the wardens' oath. Meets Brun at the inner hall after the sentry carries word of 'Sigrun's daughter'.

entries.text:
Your voice carries up the wet cliff, clear and level, and the sentry goes very still. For a long breath there is only the storm. Then the lantern swings away and you hear her shout down the wall in a voice that cracks: "Open the doors! Open the doors, and fetch the captain!"

Chains rattle, and the great bronze-banded doors groan inward on a hall of lamplight and warm air that smells of oil, stone, and bread. Wardens come hurrying out into the rain, a dozen or more, in hooded cloaks pinned with the hammer-and-three-lines brooch. They stop at the threshold and stare at you. Someone murmurs, "She has Sigrun's chin." Someone else takes Maren's other arm and gently lifts her weight from you.

Garrick keeps a pace behind you and a hand away from his bow, watching the doorways the way he watches ridgelines. A young warden eyes his longbow, then you, and says only, "He is with the Stonehearth. Let him pass."

Down the central gallery, between rows of lamps that burn without smoke (the lamp-maker's work, you realize, and your throat tightens), a broad, iron-grey dwarf is striding toward you with a cairn-stone pendant on his chest and a face that has not smiled in a long time. Torvald Greycairn stops three paces away. His eyes go to your face, to the iron ring on your finger, to the ledger under your arm, and for a moment the stern lines of his face come undone.

"Sigrun's daughter," he says, hoarse. "Forty winters, near enough, I have looked at that chin. Come in out of the rain, child." Then, more gruffly, to Maren: "You are three days late, you stubborn old crow. I had the kettle on twice."

Behind him, at the far end of the gallery, a stair of dark stone climbs toward a high arch carved with names. The Hall of Names is up there, and your father's.

You are at 21 of 21 with three spell slots and Channel Divinity, dripping on the floor of your mother's home. What does Brun do?

sheet.opening: Brunhilde "Brun" Stonehearth, a stocky Hill Dwarf cleric of the Morninglord (Life domain), auburn braid threaded with brass beads, dented but polished chain mail, warhammer worn smooth at the grip, carries the prayer book of her late foster-father figure, Father Dorrin Ashbeard, the old priest who found her as a half-starved orphan in a collapsed mine shaft outside a hill-hold and raised her in his small shrine. She is optimistic, tries to find common ground even between fierce enemies, is suspicious of strangers, and wants to repay the mercy she was shown by walking into danger to keep others alive (ideal: Charity). Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. Keep the backstory true: Father Dorrin raised her long ago and she carries his book; nothing about it is recent or lost.
